question: When moving an injured person (casualty transport), what is the main goal for a nurse?

options.A: Providing complete surgical intervention inside the ambulance
options.B: Moving the patient to definitive care without worsening their condition
options.C: Clearing the emergency department for incoming trauma victims
options.D: Accelerating discharge processes from the primary health center

explanation: You've got this! The core aim when transporting any injured person is getting them safely to a higher level of medical help while making sure you don't cause any extra harm along the way. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h1)

question: Why is it so important to check that the accident scene is safe before you try to move an injured patient?

options.A: To ensure the ambulance driver can speed through traffic safely
options.B: To comply strictly with hospital administrative safety protocols
options.C: To prevent further injury to both the patient and the nurse
options.D: To allow relatives enough time to gather personal belongings

explanation: Safety first! As a nurse, you must always check the environment so you don't end up becoming a patient yourself during the rescue. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h1)

question: What does the letter 'C' stand for in the emergency stabilization framework?
explanation: In the ABCDE emergency approach, C stands for circulation, which involves managing bleeding and assessing pulse. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h2)

question: Why is it dangerous to move a patient before stabilizing their breathing and circulation?

options.A: The transport vehicle will consume excess fuel during the journey
options.B: The patient's life-threatening conditions can rapidly deteriorate en route
options.C: The driver will find it difficult to navigate rough rural roads
options.D: The documentation forms will take longer to fill out later

explanation: Always stabilize first! Moving an unstable patient without checking their airway, breathing, and shock status can lead to a sudden emergency while traveling. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h2)

question: Which position is best for an unconscious patient who is still breathing, to stop them from choking on fluids?
explanation: Placing an unconscious breathing person on their side is a lifesaver! It keeps their airway open and lets any fluids drain safely out of the mouth. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h3)

question: Why should a patient with a suspected spinal injury be transported flat on a firm board?

options.A: To reduce the overall weight of the stretcher during loading
options.B: To make it easier for nurses to administer intramuscular injections
options.C: To ensure the patient remains fully awake throughout the entire journey
options.D: To prevent twisting of the spine that could cause permanent paralysis

explanation: Keeping the spine straight and rigid stops any movement of damaged bones, protecting the spinal cord from further harm. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h3)

question: Which device can split into two halves so you can slide it under a patient with very little movement?
explanation: A scoop stretcher is brilliant because it separates lengthwise, letting you sandwich the patient gently without needing to roll them over. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h4)

question: What is the main job of a cervical collar during emergency transport?

options.A: To prevent the patient from speaking loudly
options.B: To keep the jaw firmly closed against vomiting
options.C: To restrict movement of the neck vertebrae
options.D: To secure the oxygen nasal cannula in place

explanation: Think of a cervical collar as a seatbelt for the neck! It limits bending and twisting to protect a potentially injured spinal cord. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h4)

question: What is the correct way to use your body when lifting a heavy patient off the floor?

options.A: Bend at the knees and keep the back straight
options.B: Keep the knees locked and bend entirely at the waist
options.C: Twist the torso quickly to build momentum for the lift
options.D: Hold the patient at arm's length away from the chest

explanation: Protect your back! Always lift with the strong muscles in your legs rather than bending over your lower back. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h5)

question: Why do we need one person to count out loud when a team is moving a patient?

options.A: To measure the exact duration of the transfer procedure
options.B: To ensure everyone lifts and moves at the exact same moment
options.C: To keep the patient calm by distracting them with counting
options.D: To signal the ambulance driver when to start the engine

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Counting together (like '1, 2, 3, lift!') prevents slips, awkward drops, and extra pain for the patient. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h5)

question: Which vital signs must a nurse check constantly or very frequently while transporting a patient?
explanation: Always keep an eye on breathing and pulse! A patient's stability can change in a split second while you're on the move. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h6)

question: What is a common challenge when trying to watch intravenous (IV) infusions inside a moving ambulance?

options.A: Infusion pumps operate faster when the vehicle travels uphill
options.B: Vehicle vibrations and bumps can obscure changes or dislodge lines
options.C: The intravenous fluid bags automatically freeze due to air conditioning
options.D: Normal saline solutions change chemical composition during transit

explanation: Bumpy roads make it tough! Vibrations can mess with drip rates or pull out lines, so nurses have to be extra vigilant. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h6)

question: What does the acronym SBAR stand for in clinical handover communication?
explanation: SBAR is a standardized communication framework that ensures crucial patient details are transmitted clearly without unnecessary fluff. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h7)

question: Why is giving a structured verbal report so important when you arrive at the receiving hospital?

options.A: It allows the receiving doctor to calculate hospital billing fees
options.B: It gives the transport nurses time to rest before driving back
options.C: It replaces the need to write anything down in the patient folder
options.D: It prevents critical treatment details from being forgotten during the transition

explanation: Handovers bridge the gap! A clear report makes sure the new team immediately knows what you've done and what care the patient needs next. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T10#GNS112_U7_T10_h7)
